svg.title: Lowering as a per-link disposition over the whole chain, shown on three TraceQL pipelines, with LogQL's separate compiler drawn for comparison
svg.desc: Lowering folds left over a chain whose links are the query's own stages plus three synthesised ones: Order, Limit and Emit. Every link is asked whether it can lower given the relation accumulated so far. A link that can lower does; a link that cannot becomes residual, still applies its effect on the accumulated state, and the fold continues to the next link. The lowered links need not form a prefix. A residual link is not always work done in our own process: the response builder is residual in every chain and is nevertheless served by a second SQL statement, which the legend's third entry marks and which the design calls a cut. Pipeline A lowers everything except the response builder. In pipeline B a count stage becomes residual because it cannot accept grouped rows, and the select stage after it still lowers. In pipeline C a filter lowers only partially, which clears the exactness flag and makes the aggregate, the ordering, the limit and the response builder residual. Pipeline C has no select stage: a select needs no exactness, as pipeline B shows. Panel D is not part of the fold. It shows LogQL's own compiler, which is separate from this core and is not to be merged into it, on a chain of three line filters whose middle filter cannot be compiled: it skips that filter and still compiles the other two into the SQL, orders by the row timestamp in the SQL, applies the limit in the engine over an oversampled read, and builds the response from the rows returned, with no second statement. An earlier version of this core's fold stopped at the first refusal; measured against LogQL's compiler on that query it cost twenty-point-six times more metered bytes, which is why the fold continues past a refusal. The oracle the enumeration table compares against is a transcription of LogQL's shipped filter compiler, not the shipped function itself.
svg.text: Every link is asked. A link lowers, or becomes residual and the fold continues.
The lowered links need not be a prefix. Blocking is emergent from accumulated state — column provenance, shape, `exact` — never from position.
RESIDUAL — no SQL here, but still applies its state effect
RESIDUAL, and served by its OWN SQL part — a cut
part 0 yields Reduced — 20 (trace_id, sort_key) rows = 4,616 B, seeding part 1: the winners' root read, 20 literal ids, 100 granules. Link 5 is residual AND is part 1 — the evaluator does not run it.
B. { .service.namespace="prod" } | by(name) | count() > 2 | select(.tier) — a residual link with a LOWERED link after it
exact cleared by link 2; Emit cuts
Link 2's residual effect clears `exact`; that is what makes 4 and 5 residual, not their position. Link 3 needs no exactness, so it lowers — projecting a
column onto rows the evaluator will later drop is harmless. A prefix model would have stopped at link 2 and lost link 3's projection for nothing.
C. { .service.namespace="prod" && trace:duration > 5s } | max(duration) > 1s — the split falls INSIDE the filter
AND sql = (key=… AND val='prod' AND scope='resource') AND 1
Dropping a conjunct keeps orig ⇒ sql.
Dropping a disjunct would not: it gives a subset.
Negating an over-approximation is unsound, so
NOT refuses unless its operand was exact.
The filter still lowered as far as it could — free, and it strictly reduces rows crossing the metered hop. Measured on corpus C1, lowering the aggregate
over a superset instead would turn 333 qualifying traces into 1,000. Falls back to today's behaviour exactly. Order needs exact and Limit needs an ordering,
so both refuse; Emit is Never in every chain. C carries no select() — a select has no exactness precondition, which is panel B's case, not this one.
In B and C, as in A, Emit is residual AND is its own SQL part: Never says it cannot join THIS statement, not that no statement serves it.
D. Not this fold: LogQL's own compiler (crates/pulsus-read/src/logql/plan.rs), drawn for comparison
LogQL and TraceQL keep separate compilers, and the two are not to be merged (owner decision, #507). The query: {service_name="checkout"} |= "CONN_REFUSED" |= ip("10.0.0.1") |= "pod-044"
Solid grey: compiled into the SQL by LogQL's compiler. Dashed grey: run in the engine. This is LogQL's shipped behaviour, not the fold's dispositions, and it uses none of the core's types.
LogQL's filter compiler skips a filter it cannot compile and still compiles the filters after it. Because the filter in the engine can drop rows, the SQL cannot apply the request's
limit exactly: it reads an oversampled batch and the engine cuts it. The panels below measure what the core's fold cost when it stopped at the first refusal instead — the evidence for A–C's rule.
Measured on #507's corpus. The two literal filters together match 400 of 2,000,000 rows in the key range; the first alone matches 40,000.
round trips rows to server metered bytes rows read
the core's FIRST fold, stopping at filter 2 10 10,000 3,501,588 24,133,632
20.6x more metered bytes, 10x the round trips, 118x the rows read — a regression from an architecture whose purpose is to move fewer bytes.
The enumeration that settled the core's rule: every chain of length 3 over 15 concrete LogQL atoms, parsed with our real parser, compared against a
TRANSCRIPTION of LogQL's compile_line_filters as an oracle — not the shipped function, and not emitted SQL. An equality on the ORDERED
pushed-predicate list, not a count and not a containment. query-lowering.md 11.2 nominates the gates that replace it — wave 1, none at base.
return at the first refusal (this document's first version) 3,375 1,827 715
skip only a non-lowerable line filter, else return 3,375 1,827 463
every non-lowering link becomes residual, applies its effect, fold continues 3,375 1,827 0
